note: Opens U14. Teaches observable properties, then Arrhenius, then Brønsted-Lowry and conjugate pairs. Deliberately does NOT teach pH - that is 14.3 - and does not teach strong vs weak, which is 14.2. Sets both up. 50-minute period; last 5 minutes are cleanup/reset.

fields.headline:
14.1
Properties & Definitions
fields.subhead: Identify an acid or a base from what it does, then from what it is - and say which definition you are using.

imageSubjects.section: a pH strip turning red beside a beaker of clear liquid on a dark bench

fields.headline: One Is In Your Lunch. One Burns Skin.
fields.subhead: Lemon juice and drain cleaner sit at opposite ends of the same scale. Before we can measure it, we have to be able to name it.
fields.keyq: What does a lemon have in common with battery acid?

imageSubjects.concept: a cut lemon and a bottle of drain cleaner side by side on dark slate

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write these before we go further. Everything after this slide uses them.
fields.k1_b: A substance that gives away a hydrogen ion, H+.
fields.k2_b: A substance that takes a hydrogen ion, or supplies OH-.
fields.k3_b: A dye that changes colour depending on which one it is in.
fields.mustwrite: An acid donates H+. A base accepts H+. Everything else in this unit builds on those two sentences.

imageSubjects.aside: litmus paper strips, one red and one blue, on a worn lab bench

fields.headline: What They Do, Before What They Are
fields.subhead: You can identify both in the lab without knowing a single formula. These are observable properties.
fields.c1_b:
Taste sour - in food, never in lab.
Turn blue litmus red.
React with Zn and Mg to release H₂ gas.
Conduct electricity in water.
fields.c2_b:
Taste bitter - in food, never in lab.
Feel slippery or soapy.
Turn red litmus blue.
Conduct electricity in water.
fields.mustwrite: Both conduct electricity in water. That is your first clue that both are releasing ions.

imageSubjects.concept: zinc granules fizzing in a test tube of clear acid

fields.headline: Arrhenius: What Happens In Water
fields.subhead: The first definition, and the one that matches the lab bench. Both of these split apart the moment they hit water.
fields.a1_b:
HCl → H+ + Cl-
The H+ is what makes it an acid.
fields.a2_b:
NaOH → Na+ + OH-
The OH- is what makes it a base.
fields.a3_b: This definition only works in water - and it cannot explain NH₃, which has no OH- in it at all.

fields.headline: Two Definitions, One Is Bigger
fields.subhead: Arrhenius is not wrong. Brønsted-Lowry just covers more ground - including every case Arrhenius already handled.
fields.c1_b:
Acid: produces H+ in water.
Base: produces OH- in water.

Simple. Matches the bench.
Only works in water.
fields.c2_b:
Acid: donates a proton, H+.
Base: accepts a proton, H+.

No water required.
Explains NH₃ as a base.
fields.mustwrite: Every Arrhenius acid is also a Brønsted-Lowry acid. The reverse is not true.

imageSubjects.concept: two nested circles drawn in chalk on slate, the outer one larger

fields.headline: Finding the Acid and the Base in Any Equation
fields.subhead: Four steps. Works on every Brønsted-Lowry problem you will see this unit.
fields.s2_b: The one that lost it is the acid.
fields.s3_b: Which one gained it? That is the base.
fields.s4_b: A reactant and its product differ by one H+.

imageSubjects.band: a chalk arrow drawn across a dark slate board

fields.headline: Conjugate Pairs Differ By Exactly One H+
fields.subhead: Not two. Not a whole molecule. One hydrogen ion, every time.
fields.k1_b: HCl donates its H+. What is left behind is Cl-, its conjugate base.
fields.k2_b: NH₄+ donates an H+ and becomes NH₃, its conjugate base.
fields.k3_b: Water can donate an H+ and become OH- - or accept one and become H₃O+.
fields.mustwrite: Water shows up on both lists. A substance that can act as either is called amphoteric.

imageSubjects.aside: a single water droplet on dark glass

fields.headline: Label Every Part
fields.subhead: Use the four steps. Work it with me on the board before you write anything down.
fields.problem:
NH₃ + H₂O ↔ NH₄+ + OH-

Label the acid, the base, and both conjugate pairs.
fields.g1_b: A reversible reaction with four species.
fields.g2_b: Acid, base, and the two conjugate pairs.
fields.mustwrite: Ask which species lost a hydrogen. That is always the first question.

imageSubjects.aside: an open notebook with a blank ruled page

fields.headline: Worked Through
fields.subhead: Water is the acid here. That surprises people - it is why the definition matters more than the name.
fields.f1_b: Acid donates H+. Base accepts H+.
fields.work:
H₂O → OH-  lost a hydrogen, so water is the acid.
NH₃ → NH₄+  gained it, so ammonia is the base.
Pairs:  H₂O / OH-   and   NH₃ / NH₄+
fields.mustwrite: The same substance can be an acid in one reaction and a base in another. Read the reaction, not the name.

imageSubjects.data: a completed problem in pencil on graph paper

fields.headline: The Ones You Will Actually Meet
fields.subhead: You will see these six all unit. Learn them now and 14.2 gets easier.

imageSubjects.divider: a row of amber reagent bottles on a dark shelf

fields.headline: Six Names Worth Knowing
fields.subhead: Three of each. You do not need to memorise how strong they are yet - that is next class.
fields.c1_b:
HCl - hydrochloric, in your stomach.
H₂SO₄ - sulfuric, in car batteries.
CH₃COOH - acetic, in vinegar.
fields.c2_b:
NaOH - sodium hydroxide, drain cleaner.
KOH - potassium hydroxide, in soap.
NH₃ - ammonia, in glass cleaner.
fields.mustwrite: Goggles go on before any acid comes off the shelf. No exceptions, no matter how dilute it looks.
